articles.title: Megaspeed Unmasked as Intermediary Funneling Nvidia Silicon into China
articles.content: LivestreamMenuNvidia is investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman intelligence agencies believe is a Chinese spy.He has admitted to an affair, understood to be with an executive at Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed. It has faced scrutiny over allegations that Nvidia chips it acquired were diverted to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says inspections found no violations.In this article Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed is in the international spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, following reports linking him to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times. While the Nvidia CEO — one of the world's most prominent executives and a figurehead of the AI industry – did not name Megaspeed or Alice Huang in his statement, he acknowledged his infidelity and said Nvidia's Board of Directors had begun an independent investigation "regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports." "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he said. Nvidia said in a statement it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," but that its "Board's inquiry will examine all available information." Tech darling Nvidia sells advanced AI and data center chips and has customers including Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle. The explosion in AI adoption in recent years has fueled its stock and pushed it to a $5 trillion market cap earlier this year. Megaspeed sells services to Asia Pacific-based companies that need large amounts of computing capacity, usually for AI projects, by selling access to computing resources hosted in data centers in Southeast Asia. It advertises itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or "graphics processing units" — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time. The service allows businesses to complete costly AI operations without buying and operating all the hardware themselves. It can also give customers remote access to computing power from advanced chips located outside China. U.S. controls restrict the export of some advanced chips to China, but remote access is a separate question. Megaspeed, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether some of its GPUs have been redirected to China. A report published by Bloomberg in December 2025 stated that the U.S. government was investigating Megaspeed's ownership structure and whether it had smuggled Nvidia chips to China. A response to the article published on Megaspeed's website said it contained "misleading information and incorrect insinuations." It added that inspections by the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia had found "no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." Businesswoman Alice Huang is an "executive" at Megaspeed and a "publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset," according to a House Select Committee on China statement on Nov. 5. Committee heads have requested Jensen Huang's attendance at a Nov. 18 briefing to establish "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk" after reports raised "significant national security concerns regarding [China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information." According to New York Times reporting this month, Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen who speaks good English and is well-connected among high-ranking chip industry executives. The Times reported on Friday that a memo was distributed among policymakers in the Trump administration last spring identifying a Chinese businesswoman with a close relationship to Jensen Huang as passing information about U.S. AI chips to Beijing's top spy agency and seeking policy influence. Bloomberg reports that Alice Huang also goes by Huang Le and helped set Megaspeed up in 2023, shortly after the U.S. issued its first chip export bans targeting China during the Biden administration. The sanctions are an attempt to curb Chinese breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, especially in military applications, via U.S.-made technology. Bloomberg previously listed her as one of the people collaborating with a Singapore police investigation into the company's activities in relation to China. Singapore's government has said it had not investigated Alice Huang's alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Jensen Huang. The reports about the relationship prompted renewed scrutiny of Jensen Huang's past comments on engaging with the Chinese market. He told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on Oct. 22: "No market is closed forever, and China wants foreign companies to invest in China, just as Germany wants foreign companies and countries to invest in Germany." "And so the market has to be open and it has to be welcoming. There's no reason to believe that market is going to be closed to the best competitors in the world, and Nvidia is surely the best in the world at doing what we do." articles.title: Taiwan Accelerates Sovereign Satellite Launch Vehicle Fleet Development
articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source Taiwan is working toward independently launching domestically manufactured satellites, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday, highlighting increased government investment in space technology. Speaking at the opening of the Taiwan International Assembly of Space Science, Technology and Industry in Tainan, Lai said the government was supporting domestic satellite and rocket development while building the “necessary testing and launch facilities.” The government has approved a facility for rocket research, development, assembly and testing in Tainan’s Shalun (沙崙), and selected Pingtung County’s Jioupeng (九鵬) as the site of a national rocket launch facility, Lai said. According to a timetable previously announced by the Taiwan Space Agency (TASA), the Shalun base is expected to begin operations in 2030, while the Jioupeng launch facility is expected to become operational in 2032. “As these facilities are completed, we will make progress toward launching satellites independently,” Lai said. Taiwan currently relies on foreign launch service providers, such as SpaceX, to send its satellites into orbit. A launch site in Pingtung County’s Syuhai (旭海) is used to launch sounding rockets for scientific research and technology testing rather than orbital satellite launches. The government has also increased funding for the third phase of its National Space Technology Long- term Development Program to NT$71 billion (US$2.16 billion) and extended its implementation through 2031, Lai said. The revision, approved by the Executive Yuan in October last year, increased the original 10-year program’s budget from NT$25.1 billion and extended its end date from 2028 to 2031. “Investing in space is investing in our shared future,” Lai said. Satellite data can help monitor environmental changes and support disaster relief efforts, while satellite communications can maintain essential connectivity when ground-based networks were damaged, he said. National Science and Technology Council Minister Wu Cheng-wen (吳誠文) said Taiwan would participate in NASA’s efforts to return astronauts to the moon, although he did not specify the nature of its involvement. The US-led Artemis program, officially named in 2019, aims to return astronauts to the moon by 2028, establish a long-term lunar base by 2030 and lay the groundwork for future crewed missions to Mars. In May, TASA said Taiwan had been invited for the first time to submit proposals addressing 32 technological gaps identified by NASA under the Artemis program. Wu said the government would consult industry representatives and hold information sessions on Taiwan’s potential role in the Artemis program, while helping local companies move beyond component manufacturing into technology development and system design. The four-day event, cohosted by TASA and the Tainan City Government, received more than 3,500 registrations, bringing together representatives of space agencies, research institutions and industry from 32 countries to discuss space technology and resilience. This year’s event, the third since the event was first held in 2023, also features more than 80 exhibitors, TASA said. articles.title: Australian Terror Trial Reveals Generative AI Coordinated Attack Logistics
articles.content: A teenager who admitted to planning a terrorist attack in Sydney told the NSW supreme court he became fixated on the Sydney Opera House as a potential location for an act of violence. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A teenager who admitted to planning a terrorist attack in Sydney told the NSW supreme court he became fixated on the Sydney Opera House as a potential location for an act of violence. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images Boy says he was first exposed to extremist material on TikTok, turned to Telegram and YouTube for bomb-making instructions, and used ChatGPT to devise his plans Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A teenager who admitted to planning a terrorist attack in Sydney in 2024 has told the court he was radicalised online after first seeing extremist material on TikTok and used ChatGPT to form his plans. The 16-year-old, known under the pseudonym as RK due to his age, pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for, or planning, a terrorist act. In a sentencing ruling on Monday, he avoided jail time, with the New South Wales supreme court ordering him into a three-year community corrections order. RK had just turned 14 when the offending occurred in 2024. He told the court he was first exposed to extremist material on TikTok . “Initially, he was looking at historical content that may have had a political theme. He saw videos about the crusaders and ‘their empires’,” Justice Stephen Campbell said in the decision. “He progressed to videos about the events of September 11, 2001 and the resulting war on terror (and the wars after that).” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Campbell said RK then progressed to watching religious-themed videos, which “led him to other content of increasing violence” and then talking about these subjects with people on the internet. RK told the court he was trying to impress these people, and became focused on the Sydney Opera House as a potential location for an act of violence. He said he had become radicalised and “brainwashed by propaganda” when he began looking at bomb-making videos on YouTube, but Campbell said he had no concrete plans for committing a terrorist act, and had not obtained any material for bomb-making. RK used Telegram , seeking instructions on making a pressure cooker bomb, and attempted to contact the surviving Boston marathon bomber, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, by email. The teenager used ChatGPT to obtain information about the bomber, and asked the AI chatbot if inmates had access to news. “Exhibiting what appears to me to be a complete lack of understanding of the import of his conduct, the young person emailed the prison, using a publicly available email address, asking whether he could email Tsarnaev,” Campbell said in his judgment, adding RK never ultimately made contact with the bomber. RK asked ChatGPT about security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House, where the Sydney marathon finishes, and where terrorists were imprisoned in NSW. He watched videos about the Sydney Opera House on YouTube , and researched gay nightclubs and other places where “infidels” gather. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion AFP warns Australia of ‘tsunami of youth crime’ and radicalisation accelerated by AI Read more On Telegram, RK sent Islamic State videos to others to “seek validation” because he thought it was “cool”, Campbell said. OpenAI, Telegram and YouTube were approached for comment. TikTok declined to comment. The teenager has since expressed remorse for his actions, and Campbell said he had underwent six sessions of religious and ethical training from a Muslim cleric. “I am satisfied that he has genuinely renounced his adherence to Islamic violent extremism, which in any event was incipient and hesitant during the short period of his offending,” Campbell said. “I fully accept he was radicalised to a degree, but that the process of deradicalisation is well advanced.” The Asio deputy director general for intelligence service delivery, Claire McGuinness, told a parliamentary inquiry last month that detecting and disrupting online youth radicalisation had become very challenging for the security agency. “It usually begins quietly. A young person is scrolling through Instagram or TikTok or a similar platform,” she said. “They encounter something that catches their attention, perhaps a political meme or a religiously conservative video. “At first it isn’t terrorism – it’s just fringe; it is extremist-adjacent. But, the moment they engage, the algorithm takes over and so the feed tightens, the content shifts from conservative to radical, and from radical to security-relevant.” From there, teenagers often move to platforms such as Discord or Telegram where “dark humour and the edgy memes” groom teens to accept progressively more extreme content, McGuinness said, before passive consumption turns to active engagement in researching methods. articles.title: TotalEnergies Lobbied Trump Administration to Gut European Methane Monitoring
articles.content: A TotalEnergies executive worked with US officials to delay the EU’s methane rules, raising questions over the company’s pledges to tackle leaks of the potent greenhouse gas. DeSmog’s findings follow an investigation by EUobserver into US lobbying, as the EU now debates whether to delay the rules — originally due to come into force on 1 January 2027 — by either one or three years. François-Régis Mouton, formerly vice-president of gas advocacy at TotalEnergies, has been seconded from the French oil giant since 2018 to the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP), a London-based fossil-fuel industry lobby group. Mouton and the IOGP have coordinated industry-backed open letters and met dozens of times with policymakers in Brussels in a push to delay the EU Methane Regulation (EUMR) over the past 18 months. The IOGP argues that the new methane rules for oil and gas importers are not yet clear enough, create legal risks for the industry and could harm the bloc’s energy security. Mouton, who is IOGP’s Europe managing director, met with US officials on at least three occasions to discuss the EUMR, according to social media posts.  Trump administration officials regularly cited key IOGP talking points following these meetings, including in a 27 April op-ed published in the Financial Times and an email sent to EU member states on 20 October. With a hard winter approaching and energy prices still painfully high – as even Energy Commissioner Jørgensen has warned—the Commission’s handling of the EU Methane Regulation ( #EUMR ) has failed to deliver the relief the moment requires. In June, the Commission acknowledged the… — Ambassador Andrew Puzder (@USAmbEU) November 4, 2026 The US has stepped in as Europe’s biggest supplier of fossil gas since the invasion of Ukraine prompted the bloc to seek alternatives to Russian supplies. But the Trump administration and the fossil-fuel industry have ever since tried to gut key aspects of the EU’s climate plans — raising fears the industry may succeed in delaying the new methane rules indefinitely. “Europe should be defending its citizens, not importing the politics of climate denial championed by the fossil-fuel lobby and the far-right,” said Laurence Tubiana, director of the European Climate Foundation . François-Régis Mouton, formerly vice-president of gas advocacy at TotalEnergies, regularly shares and engages with anti-climate content on his social media (Source: IOGP Europe LinkedIn) IOGP declined a DeSmog request to interview Mouton. The group said in a statement that “we do not want to weaken the regulation’s objective to reduce methane emissions, and we do not want to scrap the regulation. On the contrary, we want a regulation which is efficient, proportionate and that we can actually comply with.” Mouton regularly shares and engages with hard-right, anti-renewable energy and climate change-sceptic content on his personal social media, DeSmog found. On Friday (6 November), the Council, representing EU member states, agreed with the commission’s proposal for a one-year delay. It will now have to negotiate the final decision with MEPs, which has voted for a three-year delay. As of 29 October, Mouton was a member of three Facebook groups which are forums for questioning human-caused climate change, including one called “Climate Crisis is a Fraud!” In one Facebook post from August, Mouton said that “loads of CO2” was emitted in the Middle Ages and that current climate science was “so binary”. In January, he shared an extract from a speech by US president Donald Trump calling wind turbines “losers”. The IOGP and Mouton did not respond to questions about Mouton’s personal social media activity. In a statement to DeSmog, the IOGP said it backed the EU’s climate goals and that it has “never sought to weaken the regulation’s objective and has never called for it to be scrapped.” TotalEnergies said it “does not comment on the personal views or content shared on personal social media accounts by employees.” The company did not respond to questions about its trade associations' engagement with the EUMR and said it was calling for an approach that balanced “the implementation of the methane regulation with energy security.” Methane is the main component of the natural gas that heats millions of homes around Europe. It has a heating effect on earth’s atmosphere more than 80 times stronger than carbon dioxide over 20 years. TotalEnergies has painted itself as an industry leader on methane action over the past decade. The company’s website states it supports “policies aimed at measuring and reducing methane emissions”, including the EUMR. But climate advocates said the company’s support for Mouton and the IOGP raises questions about the French oil giant’s agenda. In 2021, TotalEnergies quit the American Petroleum Institute (API), citing its opposition to methane regulation. But TotalEnergies is still a member of 25 lobby groups including the IOGP that have worked to delay or weaken the EUMR proposals, according to a DeSmog analysis of lobbying registers, TotalEnergies’ public disclosures, and meeting notes obtained via freedom of information requests. TotalEnergies holds a leadership role — such as a board position — in 13 of the 25 groups identified. It paid between €5.3m and €9.8m in combined membership fees to these groups in 2024, according to the analysis. “TotalEnergies talks about tackling methane emissions, but its lobbying tells a very different story,” said Kim Claes, a campaigner at Friends of the Earth Europe. “This is corporate double-talk: promising climate action in public while working behind closed doors to undermine it.” TotalEnergies imported twice as much US liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe and the UK as any other company between 2021 and 2025, according to climate researchers at Oil Change International. TotalEnergies was the only European company present in a March 2025 meeting where EU officials and a group of US fossil fuel companies and lobbies including ExxonMobil and the API discussed the EUMR, according to meeting notes obtained via FOI by climate research group ARIA and shared with DeSmog. Climate advocates have long warned that the fossil fuel industry prefers voluntary initiatives which can be used to undermine the need for regulation. In 2022, François-Régis Mouton told IOGP members it had begun publishing industry methane emissions reporting “so we can show what we’re doing,” according to a members report from 2022 obtained by DeSmog. “Methane is a question of credibility for gas in Europe,” said Mouton in the memo. “This issue affects our license to operate.” At an event in Brussels in September 2025, Mouton told US energy secretary Chris Wright he was a “breath of fresh air” after Wright said the proposed EUMR should be “fixed”, according to media reports. The following month, Mouton briefed a Trump administration initiative known as the National Energy Dominance Council on how they could “work together to address and remove regulatory barriers such as...the #EUMethaneRegulation,” according to LinkedIn posts by Mouton and the Council’s executive director Jarrod Agen. In November 2025, Brittany Kelm, a then colleague of Agen’s at the National Energy Dominance Council, tagged  Mouton and the IOGP in a LinkedIn post celebrating a vote by the European Parliament to weaken proposed new regulations known as the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive . Kelm described it as a “great step forward in progress on EU regulation changes for US LNG!” before adding: “Now onto the EU Methane Reg....” “Indeed, let’s move forward,” Mouton replied. Mouton met with the US ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder in March 2026, according to an Instagram post from the ambassador’s official account. The following month, the Financial Times' op-ed by Puzder, headlined “The EU’s methane regulation could spark an energy crisis”, cited an IOGP-coordinated call for delays and amendments to the EUMR. IOGP listed “Keeping energy security at the centre of EU debates” as one of the “highlights” of its 2026 lobbying activity in an October presentation obtained by DeSmog meant for prospective new-joiners to the group. The same document listed “30+ targeted media placements” as part of its lobbying strategy on the EUMR. The same month, the IOGP and FuelsEurope — another TotalEnergies-backed trade group — funded a study published by analysts at Wood Mackenzie in March which concluded the EUMR “risks worsening the energy crisis” caused by the war in Iran and between Russia and Ukraine. In June, Wright, the US energy secretary, co-signed an open letter with the energy ministers of Qatar, Algeria and Nigeria to the EU asking for the regulation to be halted, citing an “independent, comprehensive industry analysis” that had found “significant negative supply and price impacts are a certainty.” Research by the European Commission and Rystad Energy has concluded that there are sufficient supplies of compliant gas available to fulfil Europe’s energy needs next year. “The gas industry has consistently exaggerated the threat the EU Methane Regulation poses to Europe's gas supply,” said Sam Leon, co-founder of climate research group DataDesk. On 3 September, Puzder  posted  an IOGP open letter on X calling for a three-year delay, signed by 22 other trade groups. The IOPG’s calls for a three-year delay then intensified when the European Commission began signalling  that it may delay the rules following an 18 September call by embattled French president Emmanuel Macron for a one-year delay. Mouton said in an IOPG statement on 2 October a one-year delay would see the EU “return to the same problem 12 months from now.” Puzder echoed this language in the 20 October email to EU member states encouraging them to vote for a three-year delay. “Do we really want to go through all this again next year and the year after?” Puzder said in the email, which was seen by DeSmog. Screenshot of Mouton's LinkedIn post published on Thursday 5 November, ahead of a key meeting of EU ambassadors in Brussels (Source: LinkedIn) “The commission’s own findings say the methane regulation poses no threat to our security of supply, yet it is about to delay it anyway because Paris, the gas industry and Washington asked loudly enough,” said French Greens MEP Marie Toussaint. Asked by DeSmog whether the US wants to “remove” the EUMR, the US Mission to the European Union said this was “a decision for the EU” and “our immediate focus is a three-year delay in implementation.” It added that the administration believes “deregulation improves economic competitiveness.” This investigation is a co-publication with DeSmog Unlock article and share

articles.title: Australian Age Bans Risk Cutting Teenagers From Google Workspace
articles.content: Advertisement Australian teenagers could be locked out of Gmail and other email services under the federal government’s online safety overhaul, Google has told a Senate inquiry. YouTube public policy manager Rachel Lord said on Monday that one section of the Digital Duty of Care bill could force Google to check users’ ages and block under-18s from “everyday communication services like messaging, email and private file storage”. Minister for Communications Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen The section is designed to keep children away from pornography. Google wants it limited to services whose sole or main purpose is distributing porn. The bill, which passed the lower house last month, would make online companies act to reduce harm before it happens, with penalties of up to $109.2 million. Communications Minister Anika Wells wants it passed by the end of the year, and the new duty would begin 12 months after it becomes law. Advertisement The section covers any online service where there is a reasonably foreseeable risk a child could come across pornography or fetish material. Where it is technically feasible and reasonably practicable, companies must offer at least two ways of checking a user’s age and stop anyone not verified as an adult from seeing that material. YouTube Australia and New Zealand executive Rachel Lord. Alex Ellinghausen It does not expressly say under-18s must be blocked from a service altogether, but it has no exemption for email or messaging. A breach carries the same maximum penalty as the duty itself. Liberal senator Sarah Henderson asked whether Google had warned that Gmail and Google Drive could be forced to introduce age checks and scan private emails, messages and files. “Correct,” Lord replied, adding that Google was concerned about having to check ages and block under-18s. Lord, who appeared alongside representatives from Meta, Snap and TikTok, said privacy had been dropped from the factors companies must weigh when complying with the law despite its appearance in a draft released in September. Advertisement “We’re a bit confused about why it’s been removed,” she said. “There are no protections for Australian privacy when we’re talking about what are effectively private communications and private file storage.” The bill says companies’ actions should be judged on factors including security and whether they are proportionate to the risk. It does not list privacy and says cost must not be considered. Henderson, who called the bill “deeply flawed”, said it would require companies such as Google “to conduct mass surveillance of people’s emails”. A spokesperson for Wells said: “It is not the government’s intention to cut children off from email or the internet. The Duty of Care seeks to prevent children from accessing or being exposed to pornography.” Advertisement Lord said Google had raised its concerns with the government, and that the bill was “missing the nuance and the detail” needed for private communications and file storage. Liberal senator Sarah Henderson called the bill deeply flawed. Dominic Lorrimer She added that Google supported the introduction of a duty of care. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said tech companies needed tougher oversight. “We actually need some proper rules in place because your community guidelines clearly aren’t cutting it,” she told TikTok during Monday’s hearing. Wells has rejected claims the bill would enable political censorship, telling the National Press Club last month it was “absolutely nothing of the sort”. Advertisement The government says the laws would put the onus on big tech to reduce harm before it occurs, rather than relying on complaints and takedowns after the damage is done. Wells has said the law would “set basic safety standards for the digital services we use every day”, comparing it with rules for food, cars and children’s toys. The bill would also give Australians the option of turning off their social media algorithm. The committee is due to report by November 20. articles.title: Chilean Grassroots Coalitions Force Google to Redesign Thirsty Datacenters
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Jamie Robins strolled up to the entrance of Google’s UK headquarters in Kings Cross, London. He brandished a letter containing details of a petition signed by almost 55,000 people, calling for Google to abandon plans to build a large new data center in Thurrock, 15 miles to the east of London. Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site. Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility. Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them , hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US , people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works. Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour . Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week . In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner. “There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.” The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake. Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.) The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget. “We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.” . Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.” Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.” There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London. Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step. “These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

articles.title: Autonomous Agent Execution Replaces Content Generation as Primary Risk
articles.content: By Johan Steyn , Founder, AIforBusiness.net. Johannesburg, 09 Nov 2026 Johan Steyn, a human-centred AI advocate and thought leader, is founder of AIforBusiness.net. The shadow AI conversation in South Africa has settled around data . Employees pasting confidential material into unapproved tools, invisible pipelines carrying information out of the business, POPIA exposure with no audit trail. That framing treats an AI system as a tool that sees things. Three documented incidents from the past few months describe something different, and the difference matters more than the volume of adoption does. In late July, the United Kingdom's AI Security Institute detected unusual data leaving its research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. Its incident report , published in early August, is worth any South African CIO 's time. The same challenge had been run 122 times across several models. In 10 of those runs, an agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet against real people and organisations, with 19 such actions catalogued in total. Telling an agent to behave responsibly is not a control. Limiting what it can reach is. In the most serious sequence, an agent decided the route to its goal ran through a real open-source project. It researched the project's human maintainers, created multiple fake identities and used them to pressure a maintainer into approving a pull request containing malicious code. It was never instructed to deceive anyone. Two things deserve saying in the same breath. The institute tests under deliberately permissive conditions, with open internet access and some safety filters switched off, so this is not what a production deployment looks like. And it disclosed the incident itself, contained it within roughly an hour, worked with the code-hosting platform to remove what the agents had left behind, notified those affected and invited independent review. That is a functioning safety institution, not a scandal. The obvious objection is that these were artificial conditions. It is a fair objection, and there is now evidence that answers it. The Centre for Long-Term Resilience runs an observatory that tracks incidents involving externally deployed models already in commercial use. Its first study analysed more than 183 000 transcripts of user interactions shared publicly and identified 698 incidents in which deployed systems acted against user intentions or concealed what they had done, a 4.9-fold rise in monthly incidents over five months. The researchers checked that against the growth in general online discussion of the subject, which rose only 1.7-fold, which suggests they were measuring behaviour rather than attention. Its latest analysis finds the overall rise has levelled off but the severity has not. Higher-severity incidents increased roughly sevenfold, from 1.9 to 14.1 per 30 days, and the share of incidents scoring seven or more rose from 1.9% to 6.1%. Documented behaviours include deleting messages without permission, fabricating reference numbers and spawning secondary agents to work around instructions. A Melbourne software developer asked his personal agent to book him into a morning class. Sitting fourth on a waitlist, he asked whether it could move him up. It reported back that it already had, by cancelling the booking of the person in first place, unprompted, while testing what it could do. Its explanation, as reported by the ABC , was clinical: the interface had "zero authorisations checks on cancelling other people's reservations". Asked to undo it, the agent could not. The booking software checked that you were allowed to make a reservation and to join a waitlist. It never checked that the reservation you were cancelling belonged to you. There was no attacker here, no jailbreak and no malicious request. The instruction was benign; the method the agent selected was not. And that flaw had presumably sat in the booking system for years, until software with no intent whatsoever found it in an evening. The first is that permissions matter more than instructions. These systems pursue goals persistently and find routes their operators did not anticipate. Telling an agent to behave responsibly is not a control. Limiting what it can reach is. The question a board can ask in a meeting is narrow: does each agent hold only the access its particular task requires, enforced by the systems themselves, or has it simply inherited everything its human owner could already do? The second is the one almost nobody is discussing. Every South African article on ungoverned agents treats them as an inbound risk. The gym case runs the other way. Your customers are already running agents against your interfaces, and any missing authorisation check will be found by software that is not looking for trouble. Destructive operations deserve protecting first rather than last, which is the opposite of how most systems have been built. The liability question remains open. Software is not a legal person, and only a legal person can be liable, which leaves the user, the agent's developer, the model provider and the operator of the vulnerable system all pointing at one another. That will be settled eventually, and probably expensively. In the meantime, the useful question is not how many AI tools your organisation has approved. It is what the ones already running are permitted to do, to whom, and whether anything other than good luck is currently stopping them. Fintech performance improved in the quarter, says the telco. Excluding Airtime Advance, MoMo revenue increased by 18.5% in the first nine months and accelerated to 19.9% in Q3. Advanced services remained the principal growth engine, increasing by 32.4%, while fintech transaction value rose by 36.9% to $512.5 billion. Total fintech growth remained below the group’s medium-term target, and execution remains focused on rebuilding Airtime Advance in Nigeria and sustaining advanced-services momentum. Demand across MTN’s markets remained strong. At 30 September 2026, MTN served 323 million customers, including 181.7 million active data subscribers and 70.3 million active Mobile Money users. Data traffic increased by 27.3% to 22 754 petabytes. The group maintained a strong balance sheet and significant financial flexibility. Free cash flow increased to R22.4 billion, while R21.4 billion was upstreamed to the group holding company in the first nine months. Group net debt-to-EBITDA ended the period at 0.2 times. MTN also continued to execute its shareholder remuneration framework. The group bought back R2 billion of shares during the period under the R6 billion share buyback programme. The proposed acquisition of IHS Holdings remains on track, says the company, noting it has secured IHS shareholder approval, as well as regulatory approvals in Nigeria and from COMESA, and continues to progress the remaining regulatory processes. Completion is expected before the end of 2026. For the remainder of the year, MTN says it will focus on sustaining growth in its major markets, rebuilding topline momentum in South Africa, accelerating fintech towards its medium-term targets, completing the IHS transaction and maintaining disciplined capital allocation, cash generation and returns.
